description: We’re a team of freshmen building Terra-scope, a tool that helps people explore environmental changes using NASA Earth data. Our team works across Python data analysis, statistics, AI, and React web development. We’d love to connect with people interested in climate science, data visualization, accessible design, and making scientific evidence easier for everyone to understand.
summary:
Terra-Scope turns NASA’s Earth observation data into an interactive platform for scientific investigation. Users can explore global maps, analyze regional time series, and assess trends using Seasonal Mann-Kendall testing, Sen’s slope estimation, and multiple-testing corrections. It integrates nine different environmental variables from NASA’s GPM IMERG, GLDAS, MERRA-2, and MODIS products.
Our Contradiction Hunter analyzes differences between regions, datasets, and time periods. An evidence-grounded Gemini AI Detective explains the results in an easy-to-understand way without replacing the authoritative statistical calculations. The experimental Machine Learning Forecast Engine provides local environmental outlooks with prediction intervals, backtesting, and explicit skill warnings.
Explorer and Scientist modes help different people understand the same scientific evidence in different ways. This can be done through a guided explanation or a reproducible report.
A validation suite was developed to independently test the implemented statistical calculations across regional, gridded, and synthetic cases. Terra-Scope enables users to explore, question, and understand environmental changes on Earth through the combination of transparent data analysis, responsible AI, and accessible scientific communication.
details:
Terra-scope helps people investigate how Earth’s environmental conditions are changing. Users choose a place, a time period, and an environment variable such as rainfall, soil moisture, or temperature. The app utilizes Earth observation data from NASA resources, displays it on an interactive map, tests whether an apparent trend is statistically supported, and shows its statistics evidence. Users can inspect a time series, compare two regions, discover places with opposing trends, and ask an AI detective to explain the evidence. A separate forecast view provides seasonal outlooks with uncertainty ranges and backtest results. Findings can be saved and exported in reports that include the data source, methods, limitations, and values needed to reproduce the analysis.

The project aims to make Earth data useful to both curious members of the public, whom we call explorers, and researchers. Explorer Mode explains findings in everyday language, while Scientist Mode presents the same findings with detailed statistics and methods. Because both modes use the same evidence, people with different levels of expertise can examine and discuss the same environmental changes. Both modes also show when data is missing or a result is uncertain, helping users understand that a trend does not prove its cause. We hope Terra-scope improves public understanding of climate and environmental risks while giving researchers a tool for their use. 

We built the data pipeline and API in Python, using tools including xarray, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, FastAPI, and NetCDF. The web app uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with interactive maps and charts. The project draws on NASA products including GPM IMERG, GLDAS, MERRA-2, and SMAP, alongside other climate data sources. Its optional AI explanations use Google Gemini through the backend; a template mode remains available without an AI key. The software runs on ordinary computers and requires no custom hardware.

The project’s creative approach brings historical trend analysis, an AI conversation, and seasonal forecasting into one experience. Users can explore environmental patterns on an interactive map or 3D globe, ask the AI Detective questions about a result, compare places, and look for regions where trends differ. They can then communicate what they found through reports tailored to different audiences.

In developing the project, our team considered data quality by checking for missing observations and showing differences in coverage and resolution between sources. We considered scientific accuracy by statistically testing trends and showing the statistical evidence behind each finding, including the metrics like trend estimate, p-value, and whether the result is statistically significant. Also, we considered accessibility by creating Explorer Mode for plain language explanations and Scientist Mode for detailed statistics. Finally, We also considered trust in AI by limiting the AI Detective to explanations grounded in results calculated by the analysis system.
